_comment: Dual development/test port -- the 'AI port' at base + 1000. Feature 128,
DUALPORT-DEC-01/02. See tina4-documentation/plan/v3/features/128-dual-test-port.md
and OWNER-DECISIONS.md (Batch 5).
While a developer edits code, the main dev port hot-reloads: the browser
auto-refreshes and the reload WebSocket pushes updates. That churn is
hostile to a long-lived client -- an AI agent, a test runner, an MCP
session -- that wants a steady connection. So in debug mode the server
ALSO opens a second listener at base + 1000 serving the identical
application with the reload signal turned off. One app, two doors: the
noisy one for the browser, the quiet one for tools.
'Stable' (DUALPORT-STABLE-SEMANTICS) means CONNECTION and reload-SIGNAL
stable, never a pinned code version -- a hot-reload via
/__dev/api/reload is reflected on base + 1000 too, on the very next
request there. A tool wanting an immutable code snapshot does not get
one from this feature.
DUALPORT-DEC-01 (DUALPORT-TEST-GAP, the core of this fixture): before
this work the bound base + 1000 port had NO real test in Python, PHP, or
Ruby -- every server-boot test forced TINA4_NO_AI_PORT=true (Python's
conftest.boot_child_server, 8 Ruby specs each in their own boot env) or
tested only the toolbar-suppression UNIT (PHP's DualPortReloadTest,
whose own docblock admitted the socket behaviour was 'verified live via
tina4 serve' -- i.e. never). Node's test/aiPortRange.test.ts was the
ONLY real dual-port test of the four, and it stays exactly as it was --
a separate, narrower regression pinning a specific historical bug (an
out-of-range derived port hanging startServer()). This fixture's suites
are NEW, additional files in every language (test/dualPortContract.test.ts
in Node too), ported from aiPortRange.test.ts's real-sockets shape onto
the four case names below.
A REAL BUG was found and fixed while implementing the PHP suite
(DUALPORT-PHP-CRASH, not previously catalogued): Tina4\Server::start()
set $this->aiSocket = stream_socket_server(...) DIRECTLY, and
stream_socket_server() returns FALSE (not null) on a bind failure. The
accept loop's read-set builder tests `$this->aiSocket !== null`, and
false !== null is true, so an unreset false was fed straight into
stream_select() as an invalid stream resource on the very next loop
tick -- crashing the WHOLE PHP process, base port included, the instant
a busy AI port was actually exercised. Exactly what DUALPORT-TEST-GAP
predicted: a path with zero real coverage. Fixed by binding through a
explicit `$this->aiSocket = null;` reset on every failure branch (a
bind failure AND a caught exception) instead of leaving the FALSE the
failed bind returned sitting in the property -- see Tina4/Server.php.
DUALPORT-DEC-02 (low, both proven by a per-repo regression test, NOT
part of this shared fixture -- Python/PHP were already correct on the
Ruby item, and PHP's item is a single-file default): Ruby's CLI
resolve_config(:port) read bare PORT only, ignoring TINA4_PORT, while
Tina4.resolve_bind_port (WebServer/Tina4.run!) and Tina4.mcp_port (the
+2000 supervisor/agent proxy port -- a DIFFERENT construct from the AI
port, untouched by this feature) both already preferred TINA4_PORT --
so under `tina4ruby serve` with only TINA4_PORT set, the main/AI/
supervisor ports derived from DIFFERENT bases. Fixed to the same
TINA4_PORT > PORT > default precedence (tina4-ruby lib/tina4/cli.rb);
regression in tina4-ruby spec/dual_port_base_precedence_spec.rb. PHP's
Server::__construct defaulted port=7146, disagreeing with the
documented 7145 (bin/tina4php, App::resolveBindPort) -- masked because
every real caller passes an explicit port. Aligned to 7145; regression
in tina4-php tests/LiveReloadTest.php + tests/WebSocketTest.php
(pre-existing testServerConstructorDefaults/testServerDefaultHostPort
cases, which had been asserting the WRONG value, 7146, and now assert
7145) and tests/DualPortContractTest.php::testDefaultConstructedServerUsesPort7145.
Every case below is driven through a REAL server boot on a REAL
ephemeral port pair chosen so base + 1000 never collides with anything
already running -- NO MOCKS: Python subprocess.Popen(python app.py),
PHP proc_open(php dual_port_server.php), Ruby spawn(ruby app.rb) via
the framework's own Tina4::WebServer/Tina4.run! path, Node's real
startServer() over a real HTTP socket. Positive AND negative cases: the
no_ai_port_env and busy_ai_port cases ARE the negative controls.
Mutation-proved in all four (2026-08-13, macOS + the Linux lab):
temporarily changing each language's dual-port gate to ignore
TINA4_NO_AI_PORT turns no_ai_port_env_leaves_only_the_base_port RED --
the AI port opens anyway. Reverted. PHP's crash fix was separately
mutation-proved by reverting to the direct (bug-reproducing) assignment:
a_busy_ai_port_is_skipped_without_failing_the_base_port goes RED (the
whole process crashes instead of skipping).
The four suites carry the SAME case names in each language's own idiom
(Python snake_case function, PHP testPascalCase method, Ruby it-
description, Node assert label), which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py
normalises and matches.
feature: 128 - Dual development and test ports (the stable AI port at base + 1000)

invariants.rule: In debug mode (TINA4_DEBUG truthy) with TINA4_NO_AI_PORT unset, a real connection to base + 1000 is accepted and a known route (/health) returns its real body from the SAME in-process application -- proven by a byte match on the framework identity string (tina4-python/tina4-php/tina4-ruby/tina4-nodejs) in the response.
invariants.why: This is the feature's whole point: a stable second door onto the SAME app for a long-lived tool client. Before this fixture the second listener's socket behaviour was untested in three of four languages -- PHP's own suite admitted it was 'verified live via tina4 serve' only.

invariants.rule: A reload-WebSocket upgrade request to /__dev_reload on base + 1000 is REFUSED -- it never completes the RFC 6455 handshake (never a 101 status). The AI port is tagged at accept (a contextvar / a connection flag / a request env key / a marker) and the reload channel is gated on that tag, so an AI tool driving base + 1000 is never interrupted by its own edits. Ruby's WEBrick has no rack.hijack at all, so EVERY upgrade attempt on EITHER port answers 426 rather than reaching the AI-port-specific gate for that exact request shape; Ruby's suite additionally proves the AI-port-specific gate (RackApp dev_routes) is real and wired by comparing a PLAIN (non-upgrade) GET to /__dev_reload on both ports -- the AI port alone answers 404 'Not available on AI port'.
invariants.why: The main port's dev toolbar and reload client must never reach an AI tool's stable connection -- a live-reload firing on every AI-driven edit would defeat the whole purpose of the second port.

invariants.rule: With TINA4_NO_AI_PORT truthy, NOTHING listens on base + 1000 -- a fresh bind attempt on that exact port succeeds (proving it was never claimed) while the base port continues to serve normally. This is the NEGATIVE CONTROL: without it, a fix that merely deletes the whole dual-port feature would still pass the 'refuses reload WS' case vacuously.
invariants.why: An explicit, documented opt-out must actually opt out -- an operator or CI job that sets TINA4_NO_AI_PORT to keep a port range clear must be able to trust it.

invariants.rule: When base + 1000 is already bound by something else (pre-bound by the test itself, BEFORE the server under test even starts), the server logs a WARNING naming the busy port and continues serving the base port normally -- non-fatal, deliberately the OPPOSITE of the main port's takeover behaviour (feature 129, which kills a stale Tina4 holder to reclaim ITS port). The pre-bound listener is left completely untouched.
invariants.why: The AI port is a courtesy, not a hard requirement -- a developer running two Tina4 projects side by side, or a CI job with a crowded port range, must never have the WHOLE app refuse to start over a busy convenience port. This is also where DUALPORT-PHP-CRASH was found: PHP's busy-port path did not merely warn, it crashed the entire process (see the fixture-level comment above) -- proof that an untested 'non-fatal' path can be fatal.
